glosses: To change the direction of motion after hitting an obstacle.

examples.text: The tennis ball bounced off the wall before coming to rest in the ditch.

glosses: To move quickly up and then down (or vice versa), once or repeatedly.

examples.text: He bounces nervously on his chair.

The Black Cats contributed to their own downfall for the only goal when Titus Bramble, making his first appearance since Boxing Day, and Michael Turner, let Phil Jones' cross bounce across the six-yard box as Rooney tucked in at the back post.

glosses: To cause to move quickly up and down, or back and forth, once or repeatedly.

examples.text: He bounced the child on his knee.

glosses: To suggest or introduce (an idea, etc.) to (off or by) someone, in order to gain feedback.

examples.text: I'm meeting Bob later to bounce some ideas off him about the new product range.

glosses: To leap or spring suddenly or unceremoniously; to bound.

examples.text: She bounced happily into the room.

glosses: To move rapidly (between).

glosses: To be refused by a bank because it is drawn on insufficient funds.

examples.text: We can’t accept further checks from you, as your last one bounced.

examples.text: He tends to bounce a check or two toward the end of each month, before his payday.

glosses: To leave.

examples.text: Nobody took umbrage and bounced me out of the Union for being a pro.

glosses: To have sexual intercourse.
